newsitem.title: GUAM: Guam governor tells of plane crash horror.
newsitem.headline: Guam governor tells of plane crash horror.

text.p: Guam's governor, Carl Gutierrez, said he rescued five people from a crashed Korean airliner early on Wednesday by following the screams of injured passengers trapped in the burning wreckage.

The governor, who lives just six minutes from the jungle crash site, said he and two security aides stumbled around in shoulder-high grass with only a single flashlight to aid them when they arrived at the scene in pitch darkness.

"The fire (from the plane) was not so big, so we had to follow the sounds. It was eerie and as we got closer I heard all the screams coming from the dark spots, that we refer to as the boondocks. We had to follow the sounds," he said in a conference call with reporters.
He said the last two people he helped rescue were a Korean mother and daughter who "wouldn't let go of each other."
"They were embedded into the steel and the cushions." Eventually, a doctor "yanked" the girl out and the mother followed her, he said.
Gutierrez also pulled out an 11-year-old Japanese girl from the wreckage but flames stopped him from going back to save her mother. "The mother was dead in the flames," Gutierrez said.
One of the people he personally rescued was from the cockpit of the Korean Air Lines Boeing 747, but he did not know if it was one of the pilots.
Asked how he felt, Gutierrez said: "I don't feel like a hero. You couldn't just stand there and allow the screams to go on without doing what you had to do.
The governor said more than 200 people perished in the early-morning crash.

He also said the plane had hit an oil pipeline on the ground which caused the plane to burst into flames. However, the pipeline itself did not burn. The "black-box" flight recorder, had been recovered and was on its way to Honolulu, Hawaii, for analysis by experts.
He said there were 35 survivors from the crash, but three of them subsequently died.
Most of the survivors were in in the tail section of the plane and a few in the first-class section up front.
"The tail section was not burning, but nobody survived in the midsection," Gutierrez said.
Incredibly, one woman survived almost unscathed. "She was scratched on the leg and was walking around," he said.
The Japanese girl he rescued gave officials the telephone number of her father in Japan, but the governor said she would stay at his home on the island until her father could get to Guam.

"The girl was in very good shape, but she wouldn't let my hand go," said the governor, adding that the girl had been helping a badly-injured flight attendant who was slipping in and out of consciousness.
